questions.question: Bromine oxidises methanoic acid to carbon dioxide. Which method would NOT be suitable for measuring the progress of this reaction? A colorimetry, B electrical conductivity, C quenching and titrating with acid, D measuring the volume of gas.
questions.answer: C - quenching and titrating with acid (acid cannot titrate the acid formed; an alkali is needed)
steps: Colorimetry works because bromine is orange and is used up, so absorbance falls as the reaction proceeds.
Conductivity works because neutral reactants form H+ and Br- ions, so the conductivity changes.
Measuring gas volume works because CO2 is produced as a gas.
Quenching and titrating works only if the acid formed is titrated with an alkali; titrating with an acid gives no information about the acid produced.
So option C is the unsuitable method.

questions.question: A reactant Q forms two products. Which of four graphs shows the reaction is first order with respect to Q? (Options A-D are graphs 1-4.)
steps: First order in Q means rate is directly proportional to [Q], so a plot of rate against [Q] is a straight line through the origin.
Graph 3 (rate against [Q], straight line from the origin) shows this.
Graph 2 (rate constant whatever [Q]) is zero order; Graph 1 (straight-line fall of [Q]) is also zero order; Graph 4 shows [Q] not changing at all.

questions.question: Cisplatin is hydrolysed in a first order overall reaction. Using a graph of concentration against time, which half-life is correct? Options: A 430 min, B 460 min, C 590 min, D 600 min.
steps: Initial concentration = 20 x 10^-3 mol dm-3, so the concentration must fall to 10 x 10^-3 mol dm-3 after one half-life.
On the curve, 10 x 10^-3 is reached at about 460 min (11.0 at 400 min, 9.4 at 500 min).
Check with a second half-life: 10 -> 5 x 10^-3 occurs between about 460 and 920 min, again about 460 min, so the half-lives are constant (first order).

questions.question: The rate of reaction between Y and Z was investigated and the results tabulated. What are the orders with respect to Y and Z?
questions.answer: B: order 0 with respect to Y and order 2 with respect to Z
steps: Experiments 1 and 2: [Z] doubles (0.24 -> 0.48) with [Y] constant and the rate rises by 3.20 x 10^-2 / 8.00 x 10^-3 = 4, so 2^n = 4 and the order in Z is 2.
Experiments 2 and 3: [Y] halves (0.64 -> 0.32) with [Z] constant and the rate is unchanged, so the order in Y is 0.
Orders are Y = 0 and Z = 2, option B.

questions.question: For rate = k[NO]^2[O2], which statement is NOT correct? A third order overall; B rate units mol dm-3 s-1; C rate increases when pressure increases; D doubling [NO] and quadrupling [O2] increases rate by a factor of 8.
questions.answer: D - the rate increases by a factor of 16, not 8
steps: Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3, so A is correct.
Rate is always in mol dm-3 s-1, so B is correct.
Increasing pressure of gases increases concentration, so the rate increases; C is correct.
Doubling [NO] gives 2^2 = 4; quadrupling [O2] gives 4. Factor = 4 x 4 = 16, not 8.
So statement D is the incorrect one.

questions.question: For rate = k[NO]^2[O2], what are the units of k? Options: A dm9 mol-3 s-1, B mol3 dm-9 s-1, C mol2 dm-6 s-1, D dm6 mol-2 s-1.
steps: Rearrange: k = rate / ([NO]^2 [O2]).
Units of rate = mol dm-3 s-1.
Units of [NO]^2[O2] = (mol dm-3)^3 = mol3 dm-9.
k units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol3 dm-9) = mol-2 dm6 s-1.
This matches option D.

questions.question: Using rate = k[NO]^2[O2] with [O2] = 1.10 x 10^-2 mol dm-3, initial rate = 3.20 x 10^-3 mol dm-3 s-1 and k = 1.70 x 10^3, find the initial [NO]. Options: A 1.31 x 10^-2, B 1.71 x 10^-4, C 2.02 x 10^-3, D 4.50 x 10^-2.
steps: Rearrange the rate equation: [NO]^2 = rate / (k x [O2]).
Denominator = 18.7, so [NO]^2 = 1.71 x 10^-4 mol2 dm-6.
Take the square root: [NO] = 1.31 x 10^-2 mol dm-3.
This matches option A.

questions.question: Complete a table of values for ln k and 1/T for the rate constant of the cyclopropane to propene reaction at five temperatures.
steps: 1/840 = 1.19 x 10^-3 K-1 (3 s.f., matching the other entries).
ln(1.66 x 10^-3) = -6.40 (2 d.p., matching the other entries).

questions.question: Plot a graph of ln k against 1/T for the five data points from part (a)(i).
questions.answer: A straight line of best fit with negative gradient through the five points (1/T on the x axis, ln k on the y axis)
steps: Label the axes: x = 1/T / K-1 (e.g. 1.10 to 1.40 x 10^-3) and y = ln k (from about -12 to 0), with a scale that uses more than half of the grid in each direction.
Draw one straight best-fit line through the points (they lie almost exactly on a line) sloping down from left to right, using a ruler.

questions.question: From the graph of ln k against 1/T, determine the activation energy Ea in kJ mol-1, including the value and units of the gradient.
questions.answer: gradient about -3.3 x 10^4 K; Ea = +2.7 x 10^2 kJ mol-1 (about 270 kJ mol-1)
steps: From ln k = -(Ea/R)(1/T) + constant, the gradient of the line is -Ea/R.
Ea = -gradient x R = 3.3 x 10^4 x 8.31 = 2.7 x 10^5 J mol-1 = +2.7 x 10^2 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: The activation energy for many reactions is around +50 kJ mol-1. Comment on the value of Ea found in (a)(iii).
questions.answer: Ea (about +270 kJ mol-1) is far higher than the typical +50 kJ mol-1, so very few collisions are successful except at high temperature
steps: The value is about five times the typical +50 kJ mol-1, so the reaction has an unusually high activation energy.

A high Ea means that only a very small fraction of molecules have energy >= Ea at normal temperatures, so the reaction is very slow unless the temperature is high (the data were measured at 719-889 K).
This is consistent with the ring isomerisation needing a strained C-C bond to be broken (covalent bond fission) before the product forms.

questions.question: Explain why the rate constant k increases as temperature increases.
questions.answer: k increases because more molecules have energy at or above Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions are successful
steps: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shifts to the right and flattens.
A larger proportion of molecules now have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, Ea.
More collisions are successful, so the rate constant k increases.
Arrhenius: k = A e^(-Ea/RT), so k increases exponentially as T rises.

questions.question: Which of four diagrams shows the mechanism for the second order reaction between 1-bromoethane and aqueous potassium hydroxide?
steps: A second order reaction (rate = k[C2H5Br][OH-]) is SN2: one concerted step in which OH- and the halogenoalkane both take part in the rate-determining step.

Diagram 3 shows the OH- lone pair attacking the delta+ carbon (curly arrow from the lone pair to carbon) while the C-Br bond breaks, with a single transition state containing both Br and OH partially bonded.
Diagrams 1 and 2 show a carbocation intermediate (SN1, first order); Diagram 4 has the curly arrow drawn the wrong way (from carbon to OH-).

questions.question: For the formation of iodopropanone (propanone with iodine in acid), which statement is true? Options: A units of k are dm3 mol-1 s-1, B first order overall, C units of rate are dm3 mol-1 s-1, D doubling both concentrations quadruples the rate. The rate equation itself is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: A: the units of k are dm3 mol-1 s-1
steps: The rate equation shown on the paper is rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+], second order overall (first order in propanone and in H+).
Units of k = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^2 = dm3 mol-1 s-1, so A is true.
B is false (second order overall); C is false (rate has units mol dm-3 s-1); D is false because iodine is zero order, so doubling [propanone] and [I2] only doubles the rate.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT true? A rate increases with temperature, B rate constant increases with temperature, C adding sodium hydroxide decreases the rate, D rate is unchanged when [H+] is doubled.
questions.answer: D - the rate is not unchanged; doubling [H+] doubles the rate
steps: Raising temperature increases the rate and the rate constant, so A and B are true.
Sodium hydroxide removes H+ ions (neutralises acid), lowering the rate, so C is true.
The reaction is first order with respect to H+ (rate = k[propanone][H+]), so doubling [H+] doubles the rate.
Therefore statement D is the one that is not true.

questions.question: The hydrolysis of a bromoalkane has rate = k[RBr]. Which is most likely to be RBr? A bromomethane, B 2-bromopropane, C 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, D 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
steps: Rate = k[RBr] means the rate depends only on the bromoalkane: the reaction is first order (SN1).
In SN1 the C-Br bond breaks in the slow, rate-determining step to form a carbocation.
Tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so the tertiary bromoalkane reacts fastest by SN1.
2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary, so it is the answer.

questions.question: A graph of ln k against 1/T is plotted for a reaction. Which expression gives the activation energy Ea? Options A and C contain a minus sign and B and D a plus sign; the minus signs are garbled in the extracted text.
steps: ln k = -(Ea/R) x (1/T) + constant has the form y = mx + c with y = ln k and x = 1/T.
So the gradient m = -Ea/R and Ea = -gradient x R (the gradient is negative, so Ea is positive).
Option C.

questions.question: Plot a graph of concentration of benzenediazonium chloride against time for the 333 K experiment.
questions.answer: Concentration (y axis, 0 to 0.5 mol dm-3) against time (x axis, 0 to 400 s): a smooth falling curve through the seven points, starting at 0.500 at t = 0 and flattening out towards 0.050 at 400 s
steps: Axes: x = time / s (0 to 400), y = [C6H5N2Cl] / mol dm-3 (0 to 0.50), scales using more than half the grid.
Draw one smooth curve (not dot-to-dot) that is steep at first and gets less steep as time increases (an exponential decay).

questions.question: Determine the half-life, t1/2, from the concentration-time graph, showing working on the graph.
steps: Initial concentration = 0.500 mol dm-3, so half of this is 0.250 mol dm-3.
Draw a horizontal line from 0.250 on the y axis to the curve and a vertical line down to the time axis; this reads about 125 s.
Check: from 0.250 to 0.125 mol dm-3 takes about 125 s as well (at t = 250 s), so the half-lives are constant, consistent with first order.

questions.question: Calculate the rate constant k at 333 K using ln 2 = k t1/2. Include units.
steps: ln 2 = k x t1/2, so k = ln 2 / t1/2.
Units: s-1 (first order rate constant).

questions.question: Use the rate constant from (a)(iii) to obtain a data point (1/T, ln k) for 333 K.
steps: So the point to plot is (0.00300, -5.2).

questions.question: Plot the data point from (b)(i) on the Arrhenius graph.
questions.answer: A point plotted at x = 0.00300, y = -5.2, on the left of the existing points and above the first one, lying on the same straight trend
steps: On the 1/T axis, 0.00300 is at the 0.0030 gridline, which is 0.0001 left of the 0.0031 gridline.
On the ln k axis, -5.2 lies between the -4 and -6 gridlines, 0.8 above the -6 line.
The new point lies on the line through the other five points (the line slopes down from left to right).

questions.question: Determine the gradient of the Arrhenius graph by drawing a best-fit line, including sign and units.
questions.answer: gradient = about -1.36 x 10^4 K (accept -1.3 to -1.45 x 10^4 K)
steps: Draw a straight best-fit line through the six points (the five given plus the plotted point at 0.00300, -5.2).
Choose two points on the line that are far apart, e.g. (0.00300, -5.2) and (0.00347, -11.6).
The gradient is negative and its units are K (ln k has no units, 1/T is in K-1).

questions.question: Use the gradient from (b)(iii) to calculate the activation energy for decomposition of benzenediazonium chloride, with sign and units.
questions.answer: Ea = +1.13 x 10^2 kJ mol-1 (about +113 kJ mol-1)
steps: Gradient = -Ea/R, so Ea = -gradient x R.
Ea = +113 kJ mol-1 (positive; allow +108 to +120 for the graph reading).

questions.question: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is hydrolysed with NaOH(aq). Which suggestion about the mechanism is correct? The four options are not in the extracted text.
steps: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is a tertiary halogenoalkane, which hydrolyses by SN1.
Step 1 (slow): the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically to give a tertiary carbocation and Br-; step 2 (fast): OH- attacks the carbocation.
So the mechanism is SN1 with two steps (option D); SN2 would involve a crowded transition state at a tertiary carbon.

questions.question: Describe how the rate equations for hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes by alkali give evidence for the different mechanisms of primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes. Curly arrow mechanisms are not required.
questions.answer: Primary: rate = k[RX][OH-] shows a bimolecular SN2 step; tertiary: rate = k[RX] shows a unimolecular SN1 step via a carbocation
steps: Primary halogenoalkanes: rate = k[RX][OH-] is second order overall (first order in each reactant).
Both RX and OH- must be in the rate-determining step, so the attack and loss of halide are one concerted step (SN2).
Tertiary halogenoalkanes: rate = k[RX] is first order, so only RX is in the rate-determining step.
The C-X bond breaks first in a slow step to form a carbocation intermediate (SN1); OH- attacks in a fast second step.
The rate-determining step is unimolecular for tertiary halogenoalkanes and bimolecular for primary ones.
The different rate equations therefore show different mechanisms.

questions.question: The reaction CH3COCH3 + I2 -> CH3COCH2I + HI has rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+]. Which is a possible mechanism? Mechanism options are in diagrams not in the extracted text.
steps: The rate equation rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+] has no I2, so I2 must react after the rate-determining step.

In mechanism A, the fast equilibrium CH3COCH3 + H+ <=> protonated propanone makes the concentration of protonated propanone proportional to [CH3COCH3][H+]; the slow step then loses H+ from it, so rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+].
In B the slow step involves I2, which would put [I2] in the rate equation; C and D have I2 or I- in slow steps, so they do not fit.

questions.question: For rate = k[A]^2[B]^0, initial rate = 9.0 x 10^-5 mol dm-3 s-1 at [A] = 0.30 mol dm-3 and [B] = 0.20 mol dm-3. What is k in dm3 mol-1 s-1? Options: A 8.1 x 10^-6, B 3.0 x 10^-4, C 1.0 x 10^-3, D 5.0 x 10^-3.
steps: [B]^0 = 1, so the rate depends only on [A]: rate = k[A]^2.
Rearrange: k = rate / [A]^2.
This matches option C.

questions.question: Using the data for five initial bromate(V) concentrations, plot a suitable graph to show the reaction is first order with respect to bromate(V) ions.
questions.answer: Graph of initial rate (y axis) against [BrO3-] (x axis): a straight line through the origin
steps: Axes: x = initial [BrO3-] / mol dm-3 (0 to 0.150) and y = initial rate / mol dm-3 s-1 (0 to about 2.2 x 10^-6), using over half the grid in each direction.
Draw a ruled best-fit straight line through the points and extend it to the origin (gradient about 1.39 x 10^-5 s-1).

questions.question: State how your graph shows that the reaction is first order with respect to bromate(V) ions.
questions.answer: A straight line through the origin (rate directly proportional to [BrO3-]) shows first order
steps: For a first order reaction, rate is directly proportional to [BrO3-].
Plotting rate against [BrO3-] gives a straight line that passes through the origin.
A straight line through the origin therefore shows the reaction is first order with respect to bromate(V) ions.

questions.question: Using the second experiment's initial rate data and the first order result from (a), deduce the orders with respect to Br- and H+.
questions.answer: Br-: first order; H+: second order
steps: Runs 1 and 3: [Br-] triples (0.21 -> 0.63) with the others constant and the rate triples (4.56 x 10^-5 / 1.52 x 10^-5 = 3.0), so the order in Br- is 1.
Runs 1 and 2: [BrO3-] rises 5 times (0.062 -> 0.31), which on its own (first order) would multiply the rate by 5, while [H+] is halved (0.40 -> 0.20).
Observed rate ratio = 1.90 x 10^-5 / 1.52 x 10^-5 = 1.25 = 5 x (1/2)^n, so (1/2)^n = 1/4 and the order in H+ is 2.

questions.question: Write the rate equation for the reaction using the orders from (b)(i).
steps: Orders from (a) and (b)(i): first order in BrO3-, first order in Br-, second order in H+.
Write them as powers of the concentrations: rate = k[BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2.

questions.question: Use the Run 1 data and your rate equation from (b)(ii) to calculate k, including units.
steps: Rearrange: k = rate / ([BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2).
Units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^4 = dm9 mol-3 s-1.

questions.question: Describe how a heterogeneous catalyst such as palladium increases the rate of a reaction.
questions.answer: Reactants adsorb onto the surface, bonds weaken, and an alternative pathway with lower activation energy is provided
steps: Reactant molecules are adsorbed onto the active sites on the palladium surface.
Adsorption brings reactants close together with the correct orientation, raising the local concentration.
Bonds within the adsorbed reactants weaken, so the activation energy is lowered.
The reaction goes by an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
More molecules then have energy at or above Ea, so the rate increases; products desorb afterwards.

questions.question: For 2NO + 2H2 -> N2 + 2H2O, which statement about the mechanism is correct? The steps are shown in a diagram not in the extracted text; options A-D are: step 3 is rate determining with overall order 2 / step 3 with order 4 / step 2 with order 2 / step 2 with order 3.
questions.answer: D: step 2 is the rate-determining step and the overall order is 3
steps: The slow step (step 2) is rate-determining: rate = k[N2O2][H2].
N2O2 comes from the fast equilibrium step 1 (2NO <=> N2O2), so [N2O2] is proportional to [NO]^2.
Rate = k[NO]^2[H2], which is order 2 + 1 = 3 overall, so D.

questions.question: The decomposition of ammonia catalysed by tungsten is zero order. What is the rate equation? Options: A rate = k, B rate = k[NH3], C rate = k[NH3]^2, D rate = k[N2][H2]^3.
steps: Zero order means the rate does not depend on the concentration of any reactant.
The rate equation therefore has no concentration terms.
This is rate = k, which is option A.

questions.question: What are the units of the rate constant k for this zero order reaction? Options: A no units, B s-1, C mol dm-3 s-1, D dm3 mol-1 s-1.
steps: For zero order, rate = k, so k has the same units as rate.
Rate is measured in mol dm-3 s-1.
So k has units mol dm-3 s-1, which is option C.

questions.question: Which of the graphs represents a zero order reaction? The graph options are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: A: rate against [NH3], a horizontal line
steps: Zero order means the rate does not depend on [NH3]: rate = k.
The graph of rate against [NH3] is therefore a horizontal straight line (graph A).
B (straight line through the origin) is first order; C is an exponential fall in [NH3] (first order); D shows [NH3] not changing with time, so no reaction occurs.

questions.question: Which continuous monitoring method could be used for C4H9Cl(l) + H2O(l) -> C4H9OH(aq) + H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)? Options: A electrical conductivity, B colorimetry, C mass change, D titration with alkali.
steps: The reactants are neutral molecules; the products include H+ and Cl- ions.
The number of ions in solution increases as the reaction proceeds, so conductivity increases.
Conductivity can be measured continuously, which is required here.
Colorimetry needs a coloured species, mass change needs a gas, and titration is not continuous; so A is correct.

questions.question: Azomethane, CH3N2CH3, decomposes to N2 and C2H6 in a first order reaction. Write the rate equation.
steps: The reaction is first order with respect to azomethane only.
Nitrogen and ethane are products, so they do not appear in the rate equation.
rate = k[CH3N2CH3].

questions.question: From the concentration-time graph at 573 K, determine values for t1/2 and state whether the data confirm first order behaviour. Show working on the graph.
questions.answer: t1/2 = about 130 min (accept 125-135 min); the half-life is constant, so the data confirm first order
steps: Initial concentration = 9.0 x 10^-3 mol dm-3. Half = 4.5 x 10^-3: read across to the curve and down to the time axis, about 130 min.
A second half-life: from 4.5 x 10^-3 to 2.25 x 10^-3 takes the curve from about 130 min to about 262 min, i.e. about 130 min again (or 7.0 -> 3.5 x 10^-3 takes similar time).
Constant successive half-lives show that the reaction is first order.

questions.question: Calculate the rate constant k in s-1 for decomposition of azomethane at 573 K, using the half-life from (b)(i) and k = ln 2 / t1/2.
steps: Convert the half-life to seconds: 130 min x 60 = 7800 s.
Allow 8.6 x 10^-5 to 9.2 x 10^-5 s-1 for half-lives of 126-134 min.

questions.question: Explain why the rate constant for azomethane decomposition is higher at 623 K than at 523 K.
questions.answer: At 623 K more molecules have energy at or above Ea, so more collisions are successful
steps: Raising temperature from 523 K to 623 K increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
The proportion of molecules with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy increases.
More collisions are successful per second, so the rate constant is larger.

questions.question: Using k = 1.1 x 10^-6 s-1 at 523 K and k = 3.5 x 10^-3 s-1 at 623 K, calculate Ea (2 s.f., with units). R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1.
questions.answer: Ea = +2.2 x 10^2 kJ mol-1 (about 220 kJ mol-1)
steps: Ea/R = -8.065 / (-3.069 x 10^-4) = 2.628 x 10^4 K (the two minus signs cancel, giving a positive Ea).

questions.question: Identify on the structure of azomethane the covalent bond(s) that break in its decomposition, which has a high activation energy because of covalent bond fission.
questions.answer: The two C-N bonds (CH3-N) break; the N=N bond is retained and becomes the N2 triple bond
steps: Azomethane is CH3-N=N-CH3.
Products are N2 (N≡N) and C2H6 (C-C), so the CH3-N bonds must break.
The two C-N single bonds, one on each side, are the bonds that break.

questions.question: A graph of ln k against 1/T has gradient -4670 K. What is the activation energy? Options: A +38.8 kJ mol-1, B +38.8 J mol-1 K-1, C +562 J mol-1, D +562 J mol-1 K-1.
steps: Arrhenius: gradient = -Ea/R, so Ea = -gradient x R.
The value is positive and in kJ mol-1, so option A is correct.

questions.question: From the experimental data for hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane, deduce and justify the order with respect to 2-bromobutane and hydroxide ions.
questions.answer: first order with respect to 2-bromobutane; zero order with respect to OH-
steps: Experiments 1 and 2: [2-bromobutane] doubles (0.100 -> 0.200) with [OH-] constant and the rate doubles (1.01 -> 2.02 x 10^-3), so it is first order in 2-bromobutane.
Experiments 1 and 3: [OH-] doubles (0.100 -> 0.200) with [2-bromobutane] constant and the rate is unchanged (1.01 x 10^-3), so it is zero order in OH-.

questions.question: Write the rate equation using your orders from (a)(i).
steps: Only 2-bromobutane appears in the rate equation (first order); OH- is zero order so it is left out.

questions.question: Calculate the rate constant for Experiment 1, including units.
steps: k = rate / [CH3CH2CHBrCH3] using Experiment 1.
Units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3) = s-1.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane that is consistent with your rate equation, including curly arrows, dipoles and lone pairs.
questions.answer: SN1 two-step mechanism: slow heterolytic fission of C-Br to a carbocation, then fast attack of OH- on the carbocation
steps: Rate depends on [halogenoalkane] only, so the slow step involves only the halogenoalkane: SN1.
Step 1 (slow): show the dipole C(delta+)-Br(delta-) in CH3CH2CHBrCH3; curly arrow from the middle of the C-Br bond to Br; products CH3CH2CH(+)CH3 (the carbocation) and Br-.
Step 2 (fast): OH- with a lone pair on oxygen (and its negative charge); curly arrow from the lone pair of OH- to the C+ of the carbocation, giving CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 (butan-2-ol).

questions.question: Which of four graphs shows rate plotted against concentration for a zero order reaction? Graphs 1-4 are in a figure not in the extracted text.
steps: Zero order: the rate does not change when the concentration changes, so rate against concentration is a horizontal straight line.
Graph 3 is the horizontal line.

questions.question: Which of four graphs shows rate plotted against concentration for a first order reaction? Graphs 1-4 are in a figure not in the extracted text.
steps: First order: rate is directly proportional to concentration, so rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin.
Graph 4 is the straight line from the origin; Graph 1 is a curve (second order) and Graph 2 slopes downwards.

questions.question: Solid vanadium(V) oxide catalyses 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), deltaH = -196 kJ mol-1. Which statement is correct? Options: A V2O5 is a homogeneous catalyst; B decreasing pressure increases SO3 yield; C increasing catalyst surface area increases SO3 yield; D decreasing temperature increases SO3 yield.
questions.answer: D - decreasing temperature increases the equilibrium yield of SO3
steps: V2O5 is a solid and the reactants are gases, so it is a heterogeneous catalyst; A is false.
There are 3 mol gas on the left and 2 mol on the right; decreasing pressure favours the left, so B is false.
A catalyst changes only the rate, not the position of equilibrium, so C is false.
The forward reaction is exothermic (deltaH negative); lowering temperature shifts equilibrium to the right, so D is true.

questions.question: Deduce the rate equation for the reaction of bromate(V) ions with bromide ions in dilute acid, justifying the answer from the data, given the reaction is first order in bromate(V).
steps: Experiments 1 and 2: only [H+] doubles (0.30 -> 0.60) and the rate rises 4 times (3.36 x 10^-5 -> 1.34 x 10^-4), so the order in H+ is 2.

Experiments 1 and 3: [BrO3-] rises by 1.5 and [Br-] doubles, and the rate rises 3 times (3.36 x 10^-5 -> 1.01 x 10^-4). BrO3- is first order, giving 1.5, so [Br-] must account for the remaining 2: the order in Br- is 1.
Check with Experiment 4: BrO3- x1.5, H+ x2 (so x4) from Experiment 1 gives 6 x 3.36 x 10^-5 = 2.0 x 10^-4, which matches 2.01 x 10^-4.
So rate = k[BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2.

questions.question: Use the data from Experiment 4 and your rate equation from (a)(i) to calculate the rate constant, with units.
steps: k = rate / ([BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2) using Experiment 4.
Units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^4 = dm9 mol-3 s-1.

questions.question: Give one reason why the rate equation shows that the reaction cannot proceed in one step.
questions.answer: The orders in the rate equation do not match the stoichiometric equation (1 BrO3-, 5 Br-, 6 H+), so it must happen in more than one step
steps: A single step would give rate = k[BrO3-][Br-]^5[H+]^6; the experimental orders are 1, 1 and 2.
Also, a single step would need 12 particles to collide at the same time, which is extremely unlikely.

questions.question: For rate = k[NO]^2[H2], both reactant concentrations are tripled. By what factor does the rate increase? Options: A 3, B 9, C 18, D 27.
steps: Tripling [NO] multiplies the rate by 3^2 = 9.
Tripling [H2] multiplies the rate by 3^1 = 3.
Total factor = 9 x 3 = 27, which is option D.

questions.question: Which graph is correct for this reaction? The graphs are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D: rate against [NO]^2, a straight line through the origin
steps: Rate = k[NO]^2[H2], so rate is proportional to [NO]^2 and a plot of rate against [NO]^2 is a straight line through the origin (graph D).
B is wrong because rate depends on [H2] (first order), not constant; A shows [H2] falling in a straight line (zero order); C shows [NO] increasing with time, but [NO] is a reactant and falls.

questions.question: The mechanism has three steps: Step 1 NO + NO -> N2O2; Step 2 N2O2 + H2 -> N2O + H2O; Step 3 N2O + H2 -> N2 + H2O. Which step is rate-determining? Options: A Step 1, B Step 2, C Step 3, D cannot be deduced.
steps: The rate equation is rate = k[NO]^2[H2].
Step 1 is an equilibrium of NO with NO, giving [N2O2] proportional to [NO]^2.
If Step 2 is rate-determining, rate = k[N2O2][H2] = k[NO]^2[H2], which matches the rate equation.
So Step 2 is the rate-determining step.

questions.question: Two equations for the reaction of nitrogen monoxide and oxygen are shown. Which pair of rate equations could be correct? The equation options are not in the extracted text.
steps: Rate equations are found by experiment and do not depend on how the balanced equation is written (equation 1 is simply twice equation 2).
So both equations must have the same rate equation, with only k different.
A gives rate = k[NO]^2[O2] for both; C and D put the product NO2 in the rate equation and B gives two different rate equations for the same reaction.

questions.question: Which two methods can be used for continuous monitoring of the reaction between nitrogen monoxide and oxygen? Options: A colorimetry and titration, B colorimetry and volume change, C mass change and volume change, D mass change and titration.
steps: 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2: NO2 is brown, so the colour intensity changes and colorimetry works continuously.
Three gas molecules become two, so the total volume of gas changes and can be followed continuously.
Mass does not change in a closed system, so mass change is not a method here.
Titration is not continuous and is not needed for gases, so option B is correct.

questions.question: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is catalysed by iodide ions and the mechanism is shown in a diagram. What is the rate equation? Options: A rate = k[H2O2]^2[I-], B rate = k[H2O2][I-], C rate = k[H2O2]^2[I-][IO-], D rate = k[H2O2][IO-].
steps: Step 2 is the slow step, so rate = k2[H2O2][IO-].
IO- is an intermediate formed in the fast equilibrium step 1, so [IO-] is proportional to [H2O2][I-] (divided by [H2O], which is effectively constant).
Substituting, rate = k[H2O2]^2[I-]; an intermediate cannot appear in the final rate equation, which removes D.

questions.question: The half-life of a first order reaction is: A half the time for the reaction to be complete; B the time for the rate constant to halve; C the time for the concentration of a reactant to halve; D the time for the concentration of a product to double.
questions.answer: C - the time for the concentration of a reactant to halve
steps: Half-life, t1/2, is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value.
For a first order reaction this value is constant and independent of concentration.
The rate constant does not change during the reaction, so option B is wrong.
So option C is correct.

questions.question: Explain how adding a fixed volume of sodium thiosulfate and starch to the reaction mixture gives the rate of reaction.
questions.answer: Thiosulfate reduces iodine as it forms; the blue-black colour appears only when all thiosulfate is used, so rate = fixed amount of iodine / time
steps: Iodine is produced by the reaction as it proceeds.
Thiosulfate reacts with the iodine as it forms: 2S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2I-.
Iodine cannot be detected while thiosulfate is still present.
Once all the thiosulfate has reacted, iodine builds up and forms a blue-black starch-iodine complex.
The fixed amount of thiosulfate corresponds to a fixed amount of iodine produced, so rate = fixed amount / time taken.

questions.question: Using the student's results, deduce the rate equation for the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and iodide ions in acid.
steps: Runs 2 and 3: [H2O2] constant, [I-] doubles (0.0400 -> 0.0797) and the rate doubles (0.00181 -> 0.00364), while [H+] changes only slightly, so the order in I- is 1.
Runs 1 and 2: [I-] doubles (0.0198 -> 0.0400) and [H2O2] halves but the rate is unchanged, so doubling the iodide cancels the halving of H2O2: the order in H2O2 is 1.
Run 4 against Run 2: [H2O2] x2, [I-] x2 and [H+] x2 gives rate x4 (0.00181 -> 0.00730), so doubling [H+] has no effect and the order in H+ is 0.
Rate = k[H2O2][I-].

questions.question: Calculate the rate constant at 293 K using the results from Run 1, including units.
steps: k = rate / ([H2O2][I-]) using Run 1.
Units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^2 = dm3 mol-1 s-1.

questions.question: The rate is 4.45 times faster at 313 K than at 293 K. Calculate Ea for the reaction using the Arrhenius equation, to an appropriate number of significant figures, with units. R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1.
questions.answer: Ea = +57 kJ mol-1 (2 s.f.; 56.9 kJ mol-1 unrounded)
steps: Since rate is proportional to k, k2/k1 = 4.45 at the two temperatures.
Use ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R) x (1/T1 - 1/T2), with T1 = 293 K and T2 = 313 K.
Ea = +57 kJ mol-1 (2 s.f.).

questions.question: E + 2F -> G + H occurs by E + F -> J (slow) then J + F -> G + H (fast). What is the rate equation? Options: A rate = k[E][F], B rate = k[E][F]^2, C rate = k[F][J], D rate = k[E][F]^2[J].
steps: The rate is set by the slow step, which is E + F -> J.
The rate equation uses the reactants of the slow step: rate = k[E][F].
The intermediate J is not in the rate equation and F in the fast step does not appear.
So option A is correct.

questions.question: What can be deduced from the position of the activation energy on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve? Options: A number of particles in the rate determining step, B number of successful collisions per second, C order of reaction, D proportion of particles with sufficient energy to react.
questions.answer: D - the proportion of particles with sufficient energy to react
steps: The Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shows the spread of molecular energies.
The activation energy marks the minimum energy needed for a successful collision.
The area under the curve beyond Ea gives the proportion of particles with enough energy to react.
So option D is correct.

questions.question: Which technique can be used to follow the progress of the hydrolysis of 2-bromobutane with aqueous NaOH? Options: A colorimetry, B measurement of gas volume change, C measurement of mass change, D titration of quenched samples.
steps: 2-bromobutane and its products are colourless, so colorimetry cannot follow the reaction.
No gas is formed, so volume change is not a method.
The mass of the reactants does not change in a closed system, so mass change is not a method.
Samples can be quenched (cooled or diluted), then titrated to find the remaining OH- or the Br- formed, so option D works.

questions.question: Iodine reacts with propanone under acid conditions: first order in propanone, first order in H+, zero order in iodine. What are the units of the rate constant? Options: A dm3 mol-1 s-1, B mol dm-3 s-1, C s-1, D mol-2 dm6 s-1.
steps: Rate = k[propanone][H+]; iodine does not appear (zero order).
Rate units are mol dm-3 s-1.
[propanone][H+] has units (mol dm-3)^2 = mol2 dm-6.
k = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol2 dm-6) = dm3 mol-1 s-1, which is option A.

questions.question: For BrO3- + 5Br- + 6H+ -> 3Br2 + 3H2O, which continuous monitoring method could be used? Options: A colorimetry, B mass change, C titration with sodium thiosulfate, D volume of gas evolved.
steps: Bromine (Br2) is formed and is orange-brown.
Colorimetry measures the absorbance of this colour continuously as the reaction proceeds.
Titration is not continuous, and no gas is evolved, so B, C and D are not suitable.

questions.topic: Units Of Rate Constant Fourth Order
questions.question: For rate = k[BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2, what are the units of k? Options: A mol dm-3 s-1, B dm3 mol-1 s-1, C dm6 mol-2 s-1, D dm9 mol-3 s-1.
steps: Overall order = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.
Units of [BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2 = (mol dm-3)^4 = mol4 dm-12.
k = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol4 dm-12) = mol-3 dm9 s-1.
This is option D.

questions.question: For rate = k[BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2, all reactant concentrations are halved. By what factor does the rate change?
questions.answer: The rate decreases by a factor of 16 (rate becomes 1/16 of original)
steps: Overall order = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.
Halving each concentration multiplies the rate by (1/2)^1 x (1/2)^1 x (1/2)^2 = (1/2)^4.
(1/2)^4 = 1/16, so the rate falls to one-sixteenth of its original value.

questions.question: The first four steps of the mechanism are shown in a diagram not in the extracted text. Which is the rate-determining step? Options: A Step 1, B Step 2, C Step 3, D Step 4.
steps: The rate equation is rate = k[BrO3-][Br-][H+]^2: one BrO3-, one Br- and two H+ take part up to the rate-determining step.
Steps 1 and 2 (fast) convert BrO3- + 2H+ into BrO3H2+, and step 3 reacts BrO3H2+ with one Br-, which gives exactly this combination.
Step 4 would bring in a second Br- and so cannot be rate determining, so C.

questions.question: N2O5 decomposes in a first order reaction with half-life 1400 s at 45 C. Starting from 1.0 mol dm-3, what is the concentration after 4200 s? Options: A 0.875, B 0.500, C 0.250, D 0.125.
steps: 4200 s / 1400 s = 3 half-lives.
After each half-life the concentration halves: 1.0 -> 0.5 -> 0.25 -> 0.125 mol dm-3.
So after 4200 s the concentration is 0.125 mol dm-3, option D.

questions.question: State the final colour of the mixture containing the starch-iodine complex in the clock reaction.
steps: Starch forms a complex with iodine when iodine is present in excess of thiosulfate.
This starch-iodine complex is blue-black, which is the end point of the clock reaction.
The colour appears as soon as all the thiosulfate has been used up and free iodine is present.

questions.question: Explain why the concentration of sodium thiosulfate must be low compared with the other initial concentrations, when the reciprocal of time is used as an approximate measure of initial rate.
questions.answer: Thiosulfate must be used up quickly so that the reactant concentrations stay nearly constant over the time measured
steps: The time measured is the time for a fixed amount of thiosulfate to be used up.
If the thiosulfate concentration is low, only a small amount of iodine needs to form before the colour change.
So the other reactant concentrations change very little during the measured time.
The rate therefore stays approximately constant, so 1/time approximates the initial rate.

questions.question: Using the table of results, deduce and justify the order of Reaction 1 with respect to hydrogen peroxide, hydrogen ions and iodide ions.
questions.answer: H2O2: first order; H+: zero order; I-: first order
steps: H2O2: Mixtures 1 and 2: [H2O2] halves (5.4 x 10^-2 -> 2.7 x 10^-2), the rate also halves (5.13 x 10^-3 -> 2.56 x 10^-3 s-1), so first order.
I-: Mixtures 1 and 3: [I-] doubles (8.2 x 10^-3 -> 1.6 x 10^-2), the rate doubles (5.13 x 10^-3 -> 1.03 x 10^-2), so first order.
H+: Mixtures 1 and 4: [H+] rises 10 times (1.7 x 10^-5 -> 1.7 x 10^-4), the rate is virtually unchanged (5.13 x 10^-3 -> 4.90 x 10^-3), so zero order.

questions.question: Write the overall rate equation for Reaction 1 using the orders from (b)(i).
steps: First order in H2O2, first order in I-, zero order in H+ (so H+ is left out).
rate = k[H2O2][I-].

questions.question: All four mixtures contained 8.50 x 10^-5 mol of sodium thiosulfate. Calculate the amount of iodine that reacted with it when the colour changed.
steps: Equation: 2S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2I-.
Mole ratio thiosulfate : iodine = 2 : 1.
Moles of iodine = 8.50 x 10^-5 / 2 = 4.25 x 10^-5 mol.

questions.topic: Rate Of Reaction With Respect To H2O2
questions.question: Using the iodine amount from (b)(iii), the stoichiometry of Reaction 1 and data from Mixture 1 (total volume 0.050 dm3), calculate the rate with respect to H2O2 in mol dm-3 s-1.
steps: Amount of I2 formed in Reaction 1 in the time = 4.25 x 10^-5 mol; Reaction 1 gives 1 mol I2 per 1 mol H2O2, so 4.25 x 10^-5 mol H2O2 reacted.
Time for Mixture 1 = 195 s, so rate = 8.5 x 10^-4 / 195 = 4.4 x 10^-6 mol dm-3 s-1 (4.36 x 10^-6 unrounded).

questions.question: Calculate the rate constant of Reaction 1 using data from Mixture 1 and your answers to (b)(ii) and (b)(iv), with units.
steps: k = rate / ([H2O2][I-]) with Mixture 1 values: [H2O2] = 5.4 x 10^-2 and [I-] = 8.2 x 10^-3 mol dm-3.
Units = (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^2 = dm3 mol-1 s-1.

questions.question: Plot ln rate against 1/T, correcting for the thermometer misreading, and determine Ea in kJ mol-1 for Reaction 1.
questions.answer: Ea = about +58 kJ mol-1 (accept 54-61 kJ mol-1), found after leaving out the misread point (T = 307 K)
steps: Plot ln rate (y axis) against 1/T (x axis); the points at 1/T = 0.00300, 0.00310, 0.00325, 0.00343 and 0.00360 lie on a straight line, but the point (0.00326, -4.0) for 307 K is off the line (it should lie close to the 308 K point, but is much lower), so it is the misread one: leave it out of the best-fit line.
Ea = -gradient x R = 7.0 x 10^3 x 8.31 = 5.8 x 10^4 J mol-1, i.e. about +58 kJ mol-1 (a least-squares fit through the five points gives 57.5 kJ mol-1).

questions.question: Use your graph to deduce the temperature the student who made the error should have read.
questions.answer: about 302 K (accept 300-304 K), so the student read 307 K in error
steps: The anomalous point has ln rate = -4.0.
On the best-fit line, ln rate = -4.0 corresponds to 1/T = 3.32 x 10^-3 K-1.
T = 1 / 3.32 x 10^-3 = 302 K, so the thermometer should have read about 302 K rather than 307 K.

questions.question: Calculate the initial rate of reaction for CH3CHO decomposition at 1000 K from its concentration-time graph, showing working on the graph.
questions.answer: initial rate = 1.6 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 s-1 (accept 1.5-1.7 x 10^-4)
steps: Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 (where [CH3CHO] = 0.60 mol dm-3) and find its gradient.
The tangent runs from (0, 0.60) to about (62 min, 0): gradient = -0.60 / 62 = -9.7 x 10^-3 mol dm-3 min-1.
Initial rate = 9.7 x 10^-3 / 60 = 1.6 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 s-1 (convert minutes to seconds).

questions.question: Deduce the rate equation at 1000 K by determining two half-lives, showing working on the graph.
questions.answer: rate = k[CH3CHO] (first order), because successive half-lives are constant at about 43 min
steps: First half-life: 0.60 -> 0.30 mol dm-3 takes about 43 min (read at 0.30 on the curve).
Second half-life: 0.40 -> 0.20 mol dm-3 takes the curve from about 25 min to about 68 min, i.e. 43 min again (0.50 -> 0.25 also gives about 43 min).
Equal half-lives show the reaction is first order in CH3CHO: rate = k[CH3CHO].

questions.question: From the graph of ln k against 1/T for CH3CHO decomposition between 1000 K and 1700 K, determine Ea to three significant figures with units.
steps: ln k = -(Ea/R)(1/T) + constant, so the gradient of the line = -Ea/R.

questions.question: The hydrolysis of RX in aqueous alkali has rate = k[RX]. Which statement is true? Options: A mechanism involves a carbocation intermediate, B SN2 mechanism, C RX could be 1-bromobutane, D the main nucleophile is H2O.
questions.answer: A - the mechanism involves a carbocation intermediate
steps: Rate = k[RX] is first order in RX only, so the mechanism is SN1.
SN1 proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, so A is true.
SN2 would have a rate equation involving [OH-], so B is false.
1-bromobutane is primary and reacts by SN2, so C is false; OH- is the nucleophile, so D is false.

questions.question: Explain how the rate equations rate = k[CH3CH2CH2CH2Br][OH-] and rate = k[(CH3)3CBr] show the different mechanisms for reaction of hydroxide ions with these halogenoalkanes.
questions.answer: 1-bromobutane: bimolecular SN2 with OH- in the rate-determining step; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: unimolecular SN1 via a carbocation
steps: 1-bromobutane: rate = k[RX][OH-] is first order in each, so second order overall.
Both RX and OH- are in the rate-determining step, so the nucleophile attacks as the halide leaves (SN2, one concerted step).
2-bromo-2-methylpropane: rate = k[(CH3)3CBr] depends only on the halogenoalkane.
The C-Br bond breaks in the slow step to form a tertiary carbocation, which is then attacked by OH- (SN1).
The 2-bromo-2-methylpropane mechanism is therefore unimolecular in the rate-determining step.
The rate equations show the rate-determining step involves OH- for the primary case but not for the tertiary case.

questions.question: Give the colour change observed once all the thiosulfate has been used up in the hydrogen peroxide-iodide reaction.
steps: While thiosulfate is present, iodine formed is reduced back to colourless iodide.
Once the thiosulfate is used up, iodine builds up.
Iodine with starch gives a blue-black colour, so the colour changes from colourless to blue-black.

questions.question: Plot a graph of reaction rate (reciprocal of time) against volume of hydrogen peroxide using the table.
questions.answer: Graph of rate (y axis, 10^-2 s-1) against volume of H2O2 (x axis, cm3): a straight line through the origin
steps: Axes: x = volume of H2O2 / cm3 (0 to 50), y = reaction rate / 10^-2 s-1 (0 to 5); use more than half the grid.
Draw a ruled straight best-fit line through the origin passing close to all the points (the point at 30 cm3 lies slightly below the line).

questions.question: State and justify the order with respect to hydrogen peroxide from your graph of rate against volume.
questions.answer: First order with respect to H2O2, because the graph is a straight line through the origin
steps: Rate is directly proportional to the volume of H2O2, and the volume is proportional to its concentration (assuming the total volume is kept constant with water).
Doubling the volume doubles the rate (0.9 -> 1.8 x 10^-2 for 10 -> 20 cm3), so the order is 1.

questions.question: Using the tangent shown on the graph of the Mg and sulfuric acid reaction at 80 C, calculate the rate at 15 seconds to two significant figures with units.
steps: Rate = gradient of the tangent at t = 15 s.
The tangent passes through about (0, 15) and (33, 74): gradient = (74 - 15) / (33 - 0) = 59 / 33 = 1.8.
Units: cm3 s-1 (volume of hydrogen per second).

questions.question: The temperature is changed to 75 C. Draw on the graph the expected line if this were the only change, and justify similarities and differences.
questions.answer: A curve starting at the origin, less steep than the 80 C curve and reaching the same final volume (70 cm3) later
steps: Same start point (0, 0) and same final volume of about 70 cm3, because the amounts of reagents are unchanged.
The curve is less steep at the start and lies below the 80 C curve, so it levels off at 70 cm3 later (after more than 60 s).

Justification: at lower temperature fewer particles have energy >= Ea, so fewer collisions are successful per second and the rate (gradient) is lower; the amount of product depends on the limiting reagent, not on the temperature.

questions.question: A graph of the concentration of Q during decomposition is shown. What is the half-life? Options: A 93 min, B 132 min, C 146 min, D 291 min.
steps: The initial concentration is 9.0 x 10^-3 mol dm-3, so one half-life is reached when [Q] = 4.5 x 10^-3.
On the curve, 4.5 x 10^-3 is reached at about 132 min.
Check: 4.5 -> 2.25 x 10^-3 takes a similar time (about 130 min), so the half-life is constant.

questions.question: In an experiment to determine the rate of Br2(aq) + HCOOH(aq) -> 2H+ + 2Br- + CO2, which method would NOT be suitable? Options: A quenching and titrating with an acid, B measuring the loss in mass, C colorimetry, D measuring the volume of gas produced.
questions.answer: A - quenching and titrating with an acid (an alkali is needed to titrate the acid formed)
steps: Colorimetry works because bromine is coloured and is used up.
Mass loss works because CO2 escapes, so mass decreases as the reaction proceeds.
Gas volume works because CO2 is produced and can be collected and measured.
Quenching and titrating works only if the acid H+ produced is titrated with alkali; an acid titrant gives no information about the acid formed.
So option A is the unsuitable method.

questions.question: A chloroalkane RCl undergoes hydrolysis with rate = k[RCl]. Which chloroalkane is most likely? Options: A CH3CH2Cl, B (CH3)3CCl, C CH3CHClCH3, D (CH3)3CCH2Cl.
steps: Rate = k[RCl] is first order in RCl only, so the mechanism is SN1.
SN1 is fastest for tertiary halogenoalkanes because they form the most stable carbocation.
(CH3)3CCl is tertiary, so it is the most likely answer, option B.

questions.question: A reaction is second order in NO and first order in O2. If [NO] is doubled and [O2] is tripled, by what factor does the rate increase? Options: A 6, B 12, C 18, D 27.
steps: Doubling [NO] (second order) multiplies the rate by 2^2 = 4.
Tripling [O2] (first order) multiplies the rate by 3.
Total factor = 4 x 3 = 12, option B.

questions.question: Suggest why the reaction in a sample stops immediately when it is removed from the reaction mixture.
questions.answer: The sample is separated from the solid MnO2 catalyst and cooled, so decomposition stops
steps: The reaction is catalysed by solid manganese(IV) oxide.
When a sample is removed, it no longer contains the catalyst (or is cooled).
Without the catalyst (or at lower temperature) the decomposition effectively stops.

questions.question: State why it is not necessary to calculate the concentration of the hydrogen peroxide solution when deducing the order with respect to hydrogen peroxide.
questions.answer: Only the relative change in concentration matters, so the order can be found from the ratio of changing volumes of titrant
steps: The order is found by comparing how the rate changes as the concentration changes.
Concentration of the original H2O2 is a constant proportional factor in each sample.
Only the ratio between values matters, so the absolute value is not needed.

questions.question: Plot a graph of the volume of potassium manganate(VII) solution against time using the table of results.
questions.answer: Graph of volume of KMnO4 (y axis, 0 to 35 cm3) against time (x axis, 0 to 30 min): a smooth downward curve that gets less steep
steps: Axes: x = time / min (0 to 30), y = volume of manganate(VII) / cm3 (0 to 35), using more than half of the grid in each direction.
Join with one smooth curve (an exponential decay shape, steepest at the start).

questions.question: Use your graph to show the reaction is first order with respect to hydrogen peroxide, showing working on the graph.
questions.answer: Constant half-life of about 12 min (accept 11.5-13 min) shows first order
steps: Volume of manganate(VII) is proportional to [H2O2] in the sample, so a halving of volume is a halving of concentration.
From 32.5 cm3 to 16.25 cm3 takes about 12.5 min (t = 0 to about 12.5 min) on the curve; show the construction lines on the graph.
From 24.8 to 12.4 cm3 (t = 5 to about 17.5 min) is also about 12 min, and 18.9 to 9.45 cm3 (t = 10 to about 22 min) is about 12 min.
Successive half-lives are constant, so the reaction is first order with respect to hydrogen peroxide.

questions.question: Two possible mechanisms are proposed by students. Explain whether or not they are consistent with the reaction being first order. The mechanism diagrams are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: Mechanism 2 is consistent with first order; Mechanism 1 is not
steps: Mechanism 1: the slow step involves two H2O2 molecules (2H2O2 -> [H4O4]), so rate = k[H2O2]^2, which is second order, so it does not fit the experiment.
Mechanism 2: the slow step is H2O2 -> 2OH, involving one H2O2 molecule, so rate = k[H2O2], first order, which agrees with the experimental result.
